t.18.1: Arjuna said: O mighty-armed one, O Hṛṣīkeśa, O slayer of Keśin, I wish to know the true nature of renunciation and of relinquishment, each separately.
t.18.2: The Blessed Lord said: The sages know saṃnyāsa to be the laying aside of actions prompted by desire; the discerning declare tyāga to be the relinquishing of the fruits of all actions.
t.18.4: Hear from me my conclusion there, concerning renunciation, O best of the Bhāratas; for renunciation, O tiger among men, has been declared to be of three kinds.
t.18.3: Some wise men declare that action, being full of fault, should be abandoned; and others say that acts of sacrifice, giving, and austerity should not be abandoned.
t.18.5: Acts of sacrifice, giving, and austerity are not to be abandoned; they must indeed be performed. Sacrifice, giving, and austerity are purifiers of the wise.
t.18.6: But even these actions should be performed, abandoning attachment and the fruits; this, O Pārtha, is my decided and supreme conviction.
t.18.7: But the renunciation of prescribed action is not proper; its abandonment out of delusion is declared to be tāmasic.
t.18.8: One who abandons an action merely because it is painful, out of fear of bodily hardship, performs a rājasic renunciation and does not obtain the fruit of renunciation at all.
t.18.9: When prescribed action is performed, O Arjuna, simply because it ought to be done, abandoning attachment and the fruit as well, that relinquishment is regarded as sāttvika.
t.18.10: The relinquisher, pervaded by goodness, wise, with his doubts cut away, does not hate disagreeable action, nor does he cling to agreeable action.
t.18.11: Indeed, it is not possible for one who bears a body to abandon actions entirely; but he who abandons the fruit of action is called a true renunciant.
t.18.12: The threefold fruit of action, undesired, desired, and mixed, accrues after death to those who have not renounced, but never to those who have renounced.
t.18.13: Learn from me, O mighty-armed one, these five causes for the accomplishment of all actions, which are declared in the Sāṃkhya doctrine, the final conclusion.
t.18.14: The seat of action, and likewise the doer, the instruments of various kinds, the many distinct activities, and here divine providence as the fifth.
t.18.15: Whatever action a man undertakes by body, speech and mind, whether right or contrary, these five are its causes.
t.18.16: This being so, whoever, owing to an untrained understanding, sees the self alone as the doer, that man of perverse mind does not see.
t.18.18: Knowledge, the object to be known, and the knower form the threefold impulse to action; the instrument, the action, and the agent form the threefold composition of action.
t.18.17: He whose state of being is not egoistic, whose understanding is not tainted, even though he slays these worlds, he does not slay and is not bound.
t.18.19: Knowledge, action, and the doer are declared in the enumeration of the guṇas to be of three kinds only, according to the distinction of the guṇas; hear of these too, just as they are.
t.18.20: That knowledge by which one sees in all beings a single imperishable reality, undivided among the divided, know that knowledge to be sāttvika.
t.18.21: But know that knowledge to be rājasa which, by way of separateness, perceives in all beings manifold entities of distinct kinds.
t.18.23: Action that is prescribed, free from attachment, performed without love or hatred by one who does not crave its fruit, that is called sāttvika.
t.18.22: But that knowledge which clings to one single task as if it were the whole, without reason, without grasp of the truth, and narrow, is declared to be tāmasa.
t.18.24: But that action which is performed by one desiring the fulfilment of desires, or again by one with egotism, and with great strain, is declared to be rājasa.
t.18.25: That action which is undertaken out of delusion, without regard for its consequences, the loss and harm it causes, or one's own capacity, is said to be tāmasa.
t.18.26: The doer who is free from attachment, who does not speak of himself, who is endowed with steadfastness and zeal, and who is unchanged in success and failure is called sāttvika.
t.18.27: The doer who is passionate, eager for the fruits of his actions, greedy, violent by nature and impure, and given to joy and grief, is declared to be rājasa.
t.18.28: The doer who is undisciplined, vulgar, obstinate, deceitful, malicious, lazy, despondent, and procrastinating is said to be tāmasic.
t.18.29: Hear now, O Dhanaṃjaya, the threefold division of understanding and of steadfastness according to the guṇas, as it is declared fully and in its distinctness.
t.18.30: The understanding that knows action and renunciation, what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, fear and fearlessness, bondage and liberation, that understanding, O Pārtha, is sāttvika.
t.18.31: That understanding by which one knows wrongly dharma and adharma, and also what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, is rājasic, O Pārtha.
t.18.32: That understanding, O Pārtha, which, enveloped in darkness, regards adharma as dharma and sees all things in reverse, is tāmasic.
t.18.33: The steadfastness by which, through unwavering yoga, one holds in check the workings of the mind, the vital breath and the senses, that steadfastness, O Pārtha, is sāttvika.
t.18.35: That steadfastness by which a foolish person does not let go of sleep, fear, grief, despondency and arrogance, O Pārtha, is tāmasic.
t.18.34: But the steadfastness by which, O Arjuna, one holds fast to dharma, pleasure and wealth, craving their fruits out of attachment, that steadfastness, O Pārtha, is of the nature of rajas.
t.18.36: But now hear from me, O bull among the Bhāratas, of the threefold happiness, in which one delights through practice and reaches the end of sorrow.
t.18.37: That which at first is like poison but in the end is like nectar, that happiness is declared to be sāttvika, born of the clarity of one's own understanding.
t.18.38: That happiness which arises from the contact of the senses with their objects, which at first is like nectar but in the end is like poison, is declared to be rājasic.
t.18.39: That happiness which deludes the self both at the beginning and in its consequence, arising from sleep, sloth and heedlessness, is declared to be tāmasa.
t.18.40: There is no being, either on earth or again in heaven among the gods, that could be free from these three guṇas born of prakṛti.
t.18.41: The duties of brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, and vaiśyas, as well as of śūdras, O scorcher of foes, are distinguished according to the guṇas that arise from their own nature.
t.18.42: Tranquility, self-restraint, austerity, purity, forbearance, and uprightness, knowledge, realized wisdom, and faith in the hereafter: these are the duties of a Brāhmaṇa, born of his own nature.
t.18.43: Heroism, vigor, steadfastness, skill, and also not fleeing in battle, generosity, and the bearing of a lord: these are the duties of the Kṣatriya, born of his own nature.
t.18.44: Agriculture, cattle-tending and trade are the work of the Vaiśya, born of his own nature; and work consisting of service is likewise the work of the Śūdra, born of his own nature.
t.18.45: Each man, devoted to his own particular work, attains perfection. Hear now how one who is intent on his own duty finds perfection.
t.18.46: By worshipping through his own work Him from whom all beings have their origin and by whom all this is pervaded, a man attains perfection.
t.18.47: Better is one's own duty, though imperfect, than the duty of another well performed. Doing the work ordained by one's own nature, one incurs no sin.
t.18.48: One should not abandon the work that is born with one's nature, O Kaunteya, even though it is flawed; for all undertakings are enveloped by fault, as fire is by smoke.
t.18.49: He whose understanding is unattached everywhere, who has mastered himself, and from whom longing has departed, attains through renunciation the supreme perfection of freedom from action.
t.18.50: Learn from me in brief, O Kaunteya, how one who has attained perfection attains Brahman, which is the supreme culmination of knowledge.
t.18.52: Dwelling in solitude, eating lightly, with speech, body and mind restrained, ever intent on the yoga of meditation, and taking full refuge in dispassion.
t.18.51: Endowed with a purified intellect, holding firm and restraining the self, abandoning sound and the other objects of the senses, and casting aside attachment and aversion,
t.18.53: Having cast off egotism, force, arrogance, desire, anger and possessiveness, free from the sense of 'mine' and at peace, he becomes fit for becoming Brahman.
t.18.54: Having become Brahman, serene in self, he neither grieves nor desires; equal toward all beings, he attains supreme devotion to me.
t.18.55: By devotion he comes to know Me truly, how great I am and who I am; then, having known Me truly, he enters into That immediately thereafter.
t.18.56: Even while always performing all actions, one who takes refuge in me attains, by my grace, the eternal, imperishable abode.
t.18.57: Mentally renouncing all actions in Me, holding Me as the supreme goal, and taking refuge in the yoga of understanding, be constantly with your mind fixed on Me.
t.18.58: With your mind fixed on me, you will cross over all difficulties by my grace. But if, out of egoism, you will not listen, you will perish.
t.18.59: If, taking refuge in egoism, you think, "I will not fight," vain is this resolve of yours; your own nature will compel you.
t.18.60: O Kaunteya, bound by your own action born of your own nature, that which you do not wish to do out of delusion, you will do even against your will.
t.18.61: The Lord dwells in the region of the heart of all beings, O Arjuna, causing all beings, as if mounted on a machine, to revolve by his māyā.
t.18.62: Go to Him alone for refuge with your whole being, O Bhārata. By His grace you will attain supreme peace and the eternal abode.
t.18.63: Thus has knowledge more secret than all secrets been declared to you by me. Reflect on it fully, and then do as you wish.
t.18.64: Hear again my supreme word, the most secret of all: you are dearly loved by me, and therefore I shall tell you what is for your good.
t.18.65: Fix your mind on me, be devoted to me, sacrifice to me, bow down to me. You will come to me alone; this I truly promise you, for you are dear to me.
t.18.66: Abandoning all dharmas, go to me alone for refuge. I will free you from all sins; do not grieve.
t.18.68: He who shall declare this supreme secret among My devotees, having shown the highest devotion to Me, shall come to Me alone, freed from doubt.
t.18.67: This is never to be spoken by you to one who lacks austerity, nor to one who lacks devotion, nor to one who does not wish to listen, nor to one who speaks ill of me.
t.18.69: And there is none among men who does Me more dear service than he, nor shall there ever be another on earth dearer to Me than he.
t.18.70: And whoever will study this sacred dialogue of ours, by him I would be worshipped through the sacrifice of knowledge; such is my conviction.
t.18.71: And even the man who merely listens to it with faith and without envy, he too, released, would attain the auspicious worlds of those whose deeds are meritorious.
t.18.72: Has this been heard by you, Pārtha, with a one-pointed mind? Has your delusion born of ignorance been destroyed, Dhanaṃjaya?
t.18.73: Arjuna said: Destroyed is my delusion, and by Your grace, O Acyuta, I have regained my memory. I stand firm, my doubts gone; I will do as You say.
t.18.74: Saṃjaya said: Thus have I heard this wondrous dialogue between Vāsudeva and the great-souled Pārtha, which makes the hair stand on end.
t.18.75: By the grace of Vyāsa I have heard this supreme and secret yoga from Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Yoga, as He Himself declared it directly.
t.18.76: O King, as I recall again and again this wondrous and holy dialogue between Keśava and Arjuna, I rejoice over and over.
t.18.77: And remembering again and again that most wondrous form of Hari, great is my astonishment, O King, and I rejoice again and again.
t.18.78: Wherever there is Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Yoga, and wherever there is Pārtha, the bearer of the bow, there will surely be fortune, victory, prosperity and sound conduct; such is my conviction.
